carried-interest.text: {"explanation": "Carry is set out in the LPA's distribution provisions and usually paid to the GP's management company or to individual professionals through a carry vehicle. Whether it is paid deal by deal or only after the whole fund returns capital changes its timing and risk. It is often confused with the management fee, which is paid regardless of performance.", "related": ["waterfall", "hurdle-rate", "catch-up", "clawback", "european-waterfall"]}
carried-interest.explanation: Carry is set out in the LPA's distribution provisions and usually paid to the GP's management company or to individual professionals through a carry vehicle. Whether it is paid deal by deal or only after the whole fund returns capital changes its timing and risk. It is often confused with the management fee, which is paid regardless of performance.

nav-loan.text: {"explanation": "Lenders size the loan as a loan-to-value ratio against the portfolio's reported NAV, so diversified portfolios with audited valuations borrow more easily. Terms usually sit in the LPA, which often requires LPAC consent or caps leverage. It is often confused with a subscription line, which is secured on LP commitments and is used earlier in a fund's life.", "related": ["subscription-line", "nav", "lpac", "lpa", "dpi"]}
nav-loan.explanation: Lenders size the loan as a loan-to-value ratio against the portfolio's reported NAV, so diversified portfolios with audited valuations borrow more easily. Terms usually sit in the LPA, which often requires LPAC consent or caps leverage. It is often confused with a subscription line, which is secured on LP commitments and is used earlier in a fund's life.

waterfall.text: {"explanation": "The waterfall is written into the LPA's distribution provisions, and it applies each time the fund distributes after an exit, not just at the end. Terms vary on whether the return test runs across the whole fund or deal by deal, and on whether the catch-up is full, partial or absent. Often confused with the carry percentage, which is only the last tier.", "related": ["european-waterfall", "american-waterfall", "hurdle-rate", "catch-up", "carried-interest"]}
waterfall.explanation: The waterfall is written into the LPA's distribution provisions, and it applies each time the fund distributes after an exit, not just at the end. Terms vary on whether the return test runs across the whole fund or deal by deal, and on whether the catch-up is full, partial or absent. Often confused with the carry percentage, which is only the last tier.

catch-up.text: {"explanation": "The catch-up rate is set in the LPA's distribution provisions and varies: 100% is a full catch-up, while 50% or 80% splits each dollar with investors during the phase. Some funds have none, so carry is paid only on profit above the hurdle. It is often confused with the hurdle itself, which it follows, and with clawback, which corrects over-distribution later.", "related": ["waterfall", "hurdle-rate", "carried-interest", "clawback", "lpa"]}
catch-up.explanation: The catch-up rate is set in the LPA's distribution provisions and varies: 100% is a full catch-up, while 50% or 80% splits each dollar with investors during the phase. Some funds have none, so carry is paid only on profit above the hurdle. It is often confused with the hurdle itself, which it follows, and with clawback, which corrects over-distribution later.

clawback.text: {"explanation": "The obligation sits in the LPA and usually applies at the fund's end, though some agreements also test it at interim dates. It is typically capped at carry received after tax, and individual partners often give guarantees, sometimes joint and several. Escrow accounts or carry holdbacks are common backstops. It is often confused with a fee clawback, which recovers other payments.", "related": ["american-waterfall", "carried-interest", "waterfall", "lpa", "european-waterfall"]}
clawback.explanation: The obligation sits in the LPA and usually applies at the fund's end, though some agreements also test it at interim dates. It is typically capped at carry received after tax, and individual partners often give guarantees, sometimes joint and several. Escrow accounts or carry holdbacks are common backstops. It is often confused with a fee clawback, which recovers other payments.

hurdle-rate.text: {"explanation": "The hurdle sits in the LPA's distribution waterfall and usually compounds annually on contributed capital from the date each capital call is funded. It is often confused with a fee-style threshold, but it is a payout-ordering rule. With a catch-up, the manager can then recover carry on the whole profit; without one, carry applies only above the hurdle.", "related": ["catch-up", "carried-interest", "waterfall", "lpa", "irr"]}
hurdle-rate.explanation: The hurdle sits in the LPA's distribution waterfall and usually compounds annually on contributed capital from the date each capital call is funded. It is often confused with a fee-style threshold, but it is a payout-ordering rule. With a catch-up, the manager can then recover carry on the whole profit; without one, carry applies only above the hurdle.

american-waterfall.text: {"explanation": "Set out in the distribution provisions of the LPA, this structure is common in US venture and real estate funds and less so in buyout funds. Terms vary: some versions require recovery of realized losses and write-downs on earlier deals, which makes them closer to a whole-fund test. It is often called deal-by-deal and contrasted with the European waterfall.", "related": ["european-waterfall", "clawback", "waterfall", "carried-interest", "lpa"]}
american-waterfall.explanation: Set out in the distribution provisions of the LPA, this structure is common in US venture and real estate funds and less so in buyout funds. Terms vary: some versions require recovery of realized losses and write-downs on earlier deals, which makes them closer to a whole-fund test. It is often called deal-by-deal and contrasted with the European waterfall.

european-waterfall.text: {"explanation": "The distribution terms sit in the LPA, usually with the carry percentage, hurdle and catch-up. Because carry starts late, it often arrives near the end of a fund's life, and the clawback matters less than under a deal-by-deal structure. Often called a whole-fund waterfall, it is the usual structure in European buyout funds and is contrasted with the American, deal-by-deal waterfall.", "related": ["american-waterfall", "waterfall", "hurdle-rate", "catch-up", "clawback"]}
european-waterfall.explanation: The distribution terms sit in the LPA, usually with the carry percentage, hurdle and catch-up. Because carry starts late, it often arrives near the end of a fund's life, and the clawback matters less than under a deal-by-deal structure. Often called a whole-fund waterfall, it is the usual structure in European buyout funds and is contrasted with the American, deal-by-deal waterfall.

management-fee.text: {"explanation": "The fee is set in the LPA and usually paid quarterly or semiannually, often in advance, with drawn capital funding it. After the investment period it typically steps down or moves to a base of invested capital or net asset value. Fund-level offsets for transaction or monitoring fees often reduce it. It is distinct from carried interest, which is performance-based.", "related": ["fee-step-down", "fee-offset", "carried-interest", "lpa", "investment-period"]}
management-fee.explanation: The fee is set in the LPA and usually paid quarterly or semiannually, often in advance, with drawn capital funding it. After the investment period it typically steps down or moves to a base of invested capital or net asset value. Fund-level offsets for transaction or monitoring fees often reduce it. It is distinct from carried interest, which is performance-based.

fee-offset.text: {"explanation": "The offset is set out in the LPA's fee provisions, and the percentage varies: 100% is common in buyout funds, while some funds offset only part. Excess offsets may carry forward or be paid out at fund end. Often confused with fee waivers, where the manager gives up fees to fund its GP commitment.", "related": ["management-fee", "lpa", "fee-step-down", "gp-commitment", "ilpa"]}
fee-offset.explanation: The offset is set out in the LPA's fee provisions, and the percentage varies: 100% is common in buyout funds, while some funds offset only part. Excess offsets may carry forward or be paid out at fund end. Often confused with fee waivers, where the manager gives up fees to fund its GP commitment.

fee-step-down.text: {"explanation": "The step-down is set out in the LPA's management fee provision and is usually triggered by the end of the investment period or by the launch of a successor fund. Funds vary in whether they cut the rate, change the base, or do both. Net invested capital is often reduced by write-downs and realizations. It is often confused with a fee offset, which reduces fees by other income.", "related": ["management-fee", "investment-period", "lpa", "fee-offset", "commitment"]}
fee-step-down.explanation: The step-down is set out in the LPA's management fee provision and is usually triggered by the end of the investment period or by the launch of a successor fund. Funds vary in whether they cut the rate, change the base, or do both. Net invested capital is often reduced by write-downs and realizations. It is often confused with a fee offset, which reduces fees by other income.

gp-commitment.text: {"explanation": "The commitment is set out in the LPA and is drawn through capital calls pro rata with other investors. It is often funded partly by waiving management fees rather than paying cash, which some investors accept and others resist. It is separate from carried interest, which is a share of profits and requires no capital.", "related": ["lpa", "carried-interest", "management-fee", "key-person", "capital-call"]}
gp-commitment.explanation: The commitment is set out in the LPA and is drawn through capital calls pro rata with other investors. It is often funded partly by waiving management fees rather than paying cash, which some investors accept and others resist. It is separate from carried interest, which is a share of profits and requires no capital.

key-person.text: {"explanation": "The clause sits in the LPA and usually names two to four senior people, with a trigger tied either to departure or to a minimum share of working time. A suspension often starts automatically and lasts a set period, such as 180 days, while the GP proposes replacements for investor approval. It is separate from no-fault removal, which does not depend on any departure.", "related": ["lpa", "no-fault-removal", "investment-period", "lpac", "general-partner"]}
key-person.explanation: The clause sits in the LPA and usually names two to four senior people, with a trigger tied either to departure or to a minimum share of working time. A suspension often starts automatically and lasts a set period, such as 180 days, while the GP proposes replacements for investor approval. It is separate from no-fault removal, which does not depend on any departure.

mfn.text: {"explanation": "The MFN right usually sits in a side letter, and the manager typically delivers a disclosure of other side letters after the final close, giving a short window to elect. Carve-outs are common: LPAC seats, regulatory or tax-driven terms, and rights tied to an investor's legal status are often excluded. It is often confused with fee discounts tied to commitment size.", "related": ["side-letter", "lpa", "lpac", "final-close", "management-fee"]}
mfn.explanation: The MFN right usually sits in a side letter, and the manager typically delivers a disclosure of other side letters after the final close, giving a short window to elect. Carve-outs are common: LPAC seats, regulatory or tax-driven terms, and rights tied to an investor's legal status are often excluded. It is often confused with fee discounts tied to commitment size.

side-letter.text: {"explanation": "Side letters are usually signed at or shortly after an investor's closing, and they sit alongside the LPA and subscription agreement. Common contents beyond fees include excuse rights, LPAC seats, co-investment access, and tax or regulatory provisions for specific investor types. Often confused with amendments to the LPA, which bind every partner; a side letter binds only the parties who sign it.", "related": ["mfn", "lpa", "lpac", "anchor-investor", "management-fee"]}
side-letter.explanation: Side letters are usually signed at or shortly after an investor's closing, and they sit alongside the LPA and subscription agreement. Common contents beyond fees include excuse rights, LPAC seats, co-investment access, and tax or regulatory provisions for specific investor types. Often confused with amendments to the LPA, which bind every partner; a side letter binds only the parties who sign it.

no-fault-removal.text: {"explanation": "The right sits in the LPA and is usually separate from for-cause removal, which turns on a defined event such as fraud or material breach. Thresholds are typically measured by commitments, often excluding the GP's and its affiliates' interests, and can differ for removal versus early termination. Terms often include a notice period, a delay after the first close, and a payout of fees or carry on removal.", "related": ["lpa", "key-person", "lpac", "carried-interest", "general-partner"]}
no-fault-removal.explanation: The right sits in the LPA and is usually separate from for-cause removal, which turns on a defined event such as fraud or material breach. Thresholds are typically measured by commitments, often excluding the GP's and its affiliates' interests, and can differ for removal versus early termination. Terms often include a notice period, a delay after the first close, and a payout of fees or carry on removal.

lpac.text: {"explanation": "The committee is created by the LPA, which sets its size, how members are chosen and what it must approve. Seats typically go to larger or earlier investors, sometimes through side letters. Members act for their own institutions and are usually not paid. It advises rather than governs: it cannot direct investments or replace the manager, and it is distinct from the full investor meeting.", "related": ["lpa", "limited-partner", "general-partner", "side-letter", "key-person"]}
lpac.explanation: The committee is created by the LPA, which sets its size, how members are chosen and what it must approve. Seats typically go to larger or earlier investors, sometimes through side letters. Members act for their own institutions and are usually not paid. It advises rather than governs: it cannot direct investments or replace the manager, and it is distinct from the full investor meeting.

ilpa.text: {"explanation": "ILPA's guidance is voluntary and has no legal force. It surfaces in LPA negotiations, side letter requests and due diligence questionnaires, where investors often measure a fund's terms against its principles. Its best-known outputs are the Principles document and the reporting templates for fees, expenses and performance. Not to be confused with an LPA, which is the binding contract.", "related": ["lpa", "limited-partner", "lpac", "management-fee", "side-letter"]}
ilpa.explanation: ILPA's guidance is voluntary and has no legal force. It surfaces in LPA negotiations, side letter requests and due diligence questionnaires, where investors often measure a fund's terms against its principles. Its best-known outputs are the Principles document and the reporting templates for fees, expenses and performance. Not to be confused with an LPA, which is the binding contract.

lpa.text: {"explanation": "The LPA is negotiated between the sponsor's counsel and prospective investors before the first close, usually starting from the sponsor's draft and the private placement memorandum. Later closers sign on to the same terms. Side letters adjust it for individual investors, and amendments typically require a stated percentage of investors by interest. It is often confused with the subscription agreement, which only covers an investor's admission.", "related": ["side-letter", "lpac", "ppm", "general-partner", "limited-partner"]}
lpa.explanation: The LPA is negotiated between the sponsor's counsel and prospective investors before the first close, usually starting from the sponsor's draft and the private placement memorandum. Later closers sign on to the same terms. Side letters adjust it for individual investors, and amendments typically require a stated percentage of investors by interest. It is often confused with the subscription agreement, which only covers an investor's admission.

first-close.text: {"explanation": "The LPA usually sets a window, often 12 to 18 months, for further closes after the first. Investors admitted later typically pay their share of fees and costs back to the first-close date, plus interest, which is the job of equalization. Early investors sometimes get fee discounts. First close is often confused with the fund's formation date.", "related": ["final-close", "equalization", "anchor-investor", "lpa", "hard-cap"]}
first-close.explanation: The LPA usually sets a window, often 12 to 18 months, for further closes after the first. Investors admitted later typically pay their share of fees and costs back to the first-close date, plus interest, which is the job of equalization. Early investors sometimes get fee discounts. First close is often confused with the fund's formation date.

final-close.text: {"explanation": "The LPA sets a deadline, typically 12 to 18 months after the first close, and the GP may extend it with LPAC consent. Investors admitted after the first close usually pay a catch-up of management fees back to that date, plus interest. The close is also capped by the fund's hard cap, if there is one. It is not the end of the investment period.", "related": ["first-close", "hard-cap", "equalization", "lpa", "investment-period"]}
final-close.explanation: The LPA sets a deadline, typically 12 to 18 months after the first close, and the GP may extend it with LPAC consent. Investors admitted after the first close usually pay a catch-up of management fees back to that date, plus interest. The close is also capped by the fund's hard cap, if there is one. It is not the end of the investment period.

hard-cap.text: {"explanation": "The hard cap is set in the PPM and the LPA, usually alongside a target size, and often sits 10% to 25% above it. Raising it generally needs LPAC or investor consent and an amendment. Managers often reach it at the final close, after oversubscribed demand. It is distinct from the target, which is only a goal, and from a soft cap.", "related": ["final-close", "commitment", "first-close", "lpa", "ppm"]}
hard-cap.explanation: The hard cap is set in the PPM and the LPA, usually alongside a target size, and often sits 10% to 25% above it. Raising it generally needs LPAC or investor consent and an amendment. Managers often reach it at the final close, after oversubscribed demand. It is distinct from the target, which is only a goal, and from a soft cap.

anchor-investor.text: {"explanation": "Anchor terms are usually negotiated before the first close and written into the LPA or a side letter. Common perks include reduced fees, a share of carried interest or management company economics, co-investment rights, and a seat on the LPAC. Anchors are typical in first-time and specialized strategies. The term is sometimes confused with a seed investor, who often takes a stake in the manager.", "related": ["first-close", "side-letter", "gp-stake", "fee-step-down", "co-investment"]}
anchor-investor.explanation: Anchor terms are usually negotiated before the first close and written into the LPA or a side letter. Common perks include reduced fees, a share of carried interest or management company economics, co-investment rights, and a seat on the LPAC. Anchors are typical in first-time and specialized strategies. The term is sometimes confused with a seed investor, who often takes a stake in the manager.

placement-agent.text: {"explanation": "Agents are engaged under a written mandate, often with exclusivity and a tail period that keeps the fee payable on investors introduced during the engagement. Fees are typically paid by the management company, sometimes with an offset against the management fee. Agents are often confused with finders, and in the U.S. must be registered broker-dealers.", "related": ["first-close", "lpa", "ppm", "anchor-investor", "ddq"]}
placement-agent.explanation: Agents are engaged under a written mandate, often with exclusivity and a tail period that keeps the fee payable on investors introduced during the engagement. Fees are typically paid by the management company, sometimes with an offset against the management fee. Agents are often confused with finders, and in the U.S. must be registered broker-dealers.

re-up.text: {"explanation": "Re-ups usually come out of an investor's annual review of a manager's track record, reporting and team, and often precede or follow the first close of the successor fund. The commitment may be larger, smaller or flat versus the prior fund. Re-up rates are sometimes counted by investor number and sometimes by dollars committed, which can give different answers.", "related": ["first-close", "limited-partner", "commitment", "anchor-investor", "vintage"]}
re-up.explanation: Re-ups usually come out of an investor's annual review of a manager's track record, reporting and team, and often precede or follow the first close of the successor fund. The commitment may be larger, smaller or flat versus the prior fund. Re-up rates are sometimes counted by investor number and sometimes by dollars committed, which can give different answers.

commitment.text: {"explanation": "A commitment is made in the subscription agreement and governed by the LPA, usually at the investor's admission to the fund. It is often confused with paid-in capital, which is only the part already called. Unfunded commitments can be called during the investment period, and some can be called later for fees, expenses or follow-on investments. Defaulting investors typically face penalties.", "related": ["capital-call", "limited-partner", "lpa", "investment-period", "dry-powder"]}
commitment.explanation: A commitment is made in the subscription agreement and governed by the LPA, usually at the investor's admission to the fund. It is often confused with paid-in capital, which is only the part already called. Unfunded commitments can be called during the investment period, and some can be called later for fees, expenses or follow-on investments. Defaulting investors typically face penalties.

ppm.text: {"explanation": "The PPM is usually issued with the LPA and subscription agreement, and its summary of terms is meant to track the LPA, which controls if the two conflict. Lawyers draft it largely to support antifraud protection under securities law. It often includes a long risk-factor and conflicts-of-interest section. Managers sometimes call it an offering memorandum or confidential information memorandum.", "related": ["lpa", "ddq", "side-letter", "reg-d-506b", "first-close"]}
ppm.explanation: The PPM is usually issued with the LPA and subscription agreement, and its summary of terms is meant to track the LPA, which controls if the two conflict. Lawyers draft it largely to support antifraud protection under securities law. It often includes a long risk-factor and conflicts-of-interest section. Managers sometimes call it an offering memorandum or confidential information memorandum.

fund-of-funds.text: {"explanation": "Funds of funds are usually organized as limited partnerships with their own LPA, and often sit in the same strategy or region, such as venture or buyout. Many also buy secondaries or make co-investments alongside the underlying managers. Fee levels and carry vary and are often lower than a direct fund's. Not to be confused with a feeder fund, which invests in one fund.", "related": ["limited-partner", "feeder-fund", "management-fee", "co-investment", "lp-led-secondary"]}
fund-of-funds.explanation: Funds of funds are usually organized as limited partnerships with their own LPA, and often sit in the same strategy or region, such as venture or buyout. Many also buy secondaries or make co-investments alongside the underlying managers. Fee levels and carry vary and are often lower than a direct fund's. Not to be confused with a feeder fund, which invests in one fund.

ddq.text: {"explanation": "Most DDQs arrive after an LP's initial interest, alongside the PPM and before onsite meetings. Content ranges from investment strategy and track record to valuation, cybersecurity, ESG and business continuity. Managers typically keep a master answer set and tailor it per investor. ILPA publishes a standard template. A DDQ is separate from the AML and KYC onboarding forms completed at subscription.", "related": ["ppm", "ilpa", "limited-partner", "aml-kyc", "first-close"]}
ddq.explanation: Most DDQs arrive after an LP's initial interest, alongside the PPM and before onsite meetings. Content ranges from investment strategy and track record to valuation, cybersecurity, ESG and business continuity. Managers typically keep a master answer set and tailor it per investor. ILPA publishes a standard template. A DDQ is separate from the AML and KYC onboarding forms completed at subscription.

limited-partner.text: {"explanation": "An LP's rights and obligations sit in the limited partnership agreement and any side letter, not in the label. Limited liability usually depends on the LP staying out of management, which is why oversight is channeled through the advisory committee (LPAC) and consent votes. LPs fund capital calls over time, and a fund is often a limited partnership but can be another vehicle.", "related": ["general-partner", "lpa", "commitment", "capital-call", "lpac"]}
limited-partner.explanation: An LP's rights and obligations sit in the limited partnership agreement and any side letter, not in the label. Limited liability usually depends on the LP staying out of management, which is why oversight is channeled through the advisory committee (LPAC) and consent votes. LPs fund capital calls over time, and a fund is often a limited partnership but can be another vehicle.

general-partner.text: {"explanation": "In a limited partnership, the GP is usually a separate legal entity from the management company that employs the investment team, and it often has unlimited liability for the fund's obligations, typically through a special-purpose vehicle. Its powers and limits are set out in the LPA. It is often confused with the manager, and it is the counterparty to the limited partners.", "related": ["limited-partner", "lpa", "gp-commitment", "carried-interest", "key-person"]}
general-partner.explanation: In a limited partnership, the GP is usually a separate legal entity from the management company that employs the investment team, and it often has unlimited liability for the fund's obligations, typically through a special-purpose vehicle. Its powers and limits are set out in the LPA. It is often confused with the manager, and it is the counterparty to the limited partners.

capital-call.text: {"explanation": "Calls fund new investments, fees and fund expenses, and the notice states the amount, purpose and due date. Each investor pays its pro rata share, and the LPA sets the notice period and default remedies, such as forfeiting part of the interest. Funds often bridge calls with a subscription line, which delays the cash needed from investors. Not the same as a distribution.", "related": ["commitment", "subscription-line", "lpa", "investment-period", "recycling"]}
capital-call.explanation: Calls fund new investments, fees and fund expenses, and the notice states the amount, purpose and due date. Each investor pays its pro rata share, and the LPA sets the notice period and default remedies, such as forfeiting part of the interest. Funds often bridge calls with a subscription line, which delays the cash needed from investors. Not the same as a distribution.

investment-period.text: {"explanation": "The investment period is set in the LPA and runs from the first close or initial closing date. It often ends early if a successor fund begins investing or the key-person provisions are triggered, and the LPA may allow an extension with LPAC consent. Some funds permit follow-ons and recycling afterward. It is often called the commitment period.", "related": ["lpa", "fee-step-down", "recycling", "key-person", "capital-call"]}
investment-period.explanation: The investment period is set in the LPA and runs from the first close or initial closing date. It often ends early if a successor fund begins investing or the key-person provisions are triggered, and the LPA may allow an extension with LPAC consent. Some funds permit follow-ons and recycling afterward. It is often called the commitment period.

recycling.text: {"explanation": "Recycling rights sit in the LPA and vary in scope. Some funds recycle only proceeds from investments sold within a set period, often the investment period, or only the cost of those investments. Others also recycle returned fees or expenses. A cap, often a share of commitments, limits the total. It differs from recallable distributions, which are returned capital that investors must fund again.", "related": ["investment-period", "lpa", "capital-call", "commitment", "dpi"]}
recycling.explanation: Recycling rights sit in the LPA and vary in scope. Some funds recycle only proceeds from investments sold within a set period, often the investment period, or only the cost of those investments. Others also recycle returned fees or expenses. A cap, often a share of commitments, limits the total. It differs from recallable distributions, which are returned capital that investors must fund again.

subscription-line.text: {"explanation": "The facility is set out in the LPA, which caps borrowing and how long a draw can stay outstanding, often 90 to 180 days. Lenders underwrite the investors' creditworthiness and their obligation to fund, not the portfolio. Also called a capital call line or credit facility. Distinct from a NAV loan, which is secured on portfolio assets.", "related": ["capital-call", "nav-loan", "irr", "commitment", "lpa"]}
subscription-line.explanation: The facility is set out in the LPA, which caps borrowing and how long a draw can stay outstanding, often 90 to 180 days. Lenders underwrite the investors' creditworthiness and their obligation to fund, not the portfolio. Also called a capital call line or credit facility. Distinct from a NAV loan, which is secured on portfolio assets.

continuation-vehicle.text: {"explanation": "Usually run as a single-asset or multi-asset deal, the vehicle is typically funded by new secondary investors, often led by one investor who sets the price. The manager normally commits fresh capital and resets carry terms. An LPAC usually must approve the conflict, and a fairness opinion is common. It is a type of GP-led secondary.", "related": ["gp-led-secondary", "lpac", "fair-value", "lp-led-secondary", "carried-interest"]}
continuation-vehicle.explanation: Usually run as a single-asset or multi-asset deal, the vehicle is typically funded by new secondary investors, often led by one investor who sets the price. The manager normally commits fresh capital and resets carry terms. An LPAC usually must approve the conflict, and a fairness opinion is common. It is a type of GP-led secondary.

gp-led-secondary.text: {"explanation": "Typically arises near the end of a fund's term, when the manager wants more time to hold a strong asset. A third-party price is usually set through a competitive process, often with a fairness opinion, and the LPAC is commonly asked to approve the conflict. Rolling investors often get new terms. Distinct from an LP-led secondary, where an investor sells its own fund interest.", "related": ["continuation-vehicle", "lp-led-secondary", "lpac", "fair-value", "tender-offer"]}
gp-led-secondary.explanation: Typically arises near the end of a fund's term, when the manager wants more time to hold a strong asset. A third-party price is usually set through a competitive process, often with a fairness opinion, and the LPAC is commonly asked to approve the conflict. Rolling investors often get new terms. Distinct from an LP-led secondary, where an investor sells its own fund interest.

lp-led-secondary.text: {"explanation": "Pricing is usually quoted as a percentage of the latest reported NAV, adjusted for cash flows since that date. The GP typically must consent to the transfer under the LPA, and the buyer takes on any unfunded commitment. Often confused with a GP-led secondary, where the manager runs the process, usually moving assets into a continuation vehicle.", "related": ["gp-led-secondary", "nav", "commitment", "tender-offer", "lpa"]}
lp-led-secondary.explanation: Pricing is usually quoted as a percentage of the latest reported NAV, adjusted for cash flows since that date. The GP typically must consent to the transfer under the LPA, and the buyer takes on any unfunded commitment. Often confused with a GP-led secondary, where the manager runs the process, usually moving assets into a continuation vehicle.

tender-offer.text: {"explanation": "In private markets, tender offers are most common in secondaries, where a buyer or the manager offers to purchase LP interests, and in public-company deals, where an acquirer goes straight to shareholders. Terms usually include a minimum acceptance level and can be extended.
